clause: §9.1(“notwithstanding” cap) read against §10.1 (IP indemnity); carve-outs in §9.3
issue: Section 10.1 says the IP infringement indemnity is “uncapped,” but §9.1 caps “any ... liability” at 12 months’ fees and opens with “NOTWITHSTANDING ANYTHING TO THE CONTRARY IN THIS AGREEMENT.” Read together, the indemnity is actually capped at ~$222,000 (12-month fees, rolling; $247,000 at most in year 1 if the $25,000 implementation fee counts as “fees paid”) — nowhere near real IP-litigation exposure. The defect is confirmed by the interpretation library: an “uncapped” statement elsewhere does not override a cap expressly made to apply “notwithstanding anything to the contrary” unless the cap clause itself carves the obligation out — and §9.3’s carve-outs (gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, customer payment obligations) do not mention §10.1. Survival is fine (§12.3 keeps §10 alive); the cap is the only problem.
why: A1 is a hard rule: the vendor’s IP infringement indemnity must survive and sit outside the liability cap. As drafted the “notwithstanding” language swallows the “uncapped” promise — this is exactly the trap the interpretation library (contract_interpretation_notwithstanding.md, citing Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ and Delaware “notwithstanding” cases) warns about. A patent/copyright claim against Cobalt from use of the platform would be Cobalt’s loss above ~$222,000. This is the single largest contingent exposure on the deal.
redline: Amend §9.3 (carve-out must sit inside the cap clause itself, per contract_interpretation_notwithstanding.md): “The exclusions and limitations in this Section 9 shall not apply to: (i) a party’s liability for its gross negligence, willful misconduct, or fraud; (ii) Provider’s indemnification obligations under Section 10.1; or (iii) Customer’s payment obligations.” And conform §10.1’s final phrase: “Provider’s obligations under this Section 10.1 are uncapped and are not subject to the limitations in Section 9.”

issue: The data processing addendum does not exist — §5.3 says the parties “shall enter into” a DPA “in the form to be attached as Exhibit C,” and Exhibit C literally reads “[To be attached.]” Client-confirmed processing scope makes this live from day one: driver names, locations and hours, and EU customer addresses from the Rotterdam/Hamburg operations run through the Europe B.V. (which, with the client’s chosen signing structure, is a Customer party to the MSA). Signing without an executed, attached DPA leaves Cobalt in breach of the Art. 28(3) processing-contract requirement “from the first day of processing” (gdpr_art28.md). “To be attached” is expressly not acceptable under A2.
why: A2 is a hard rule: DPA executed at signing whenever personal data of EU/UK residents is processed — now confirmed to include driver names, locations, hours and EU customer addresses (data subjects: drivers and customers of the EU operations). The library (gdpr_art28.md, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Art. 28(3)) requires the processing contract to set out subject-matter, duration, nature/purpose, data types, data-subject categories, controller rights/obligations, and to stipulate (a) processing only on documented instructions, (b) confidentiality, (c) security measures, (d) sub-processor conditions, (e)–(f) assistance to the controller, (g) deletion or return, and (h) information and audits. Without it, Cobalt is non-compliant from go-live.
redline: Replace §5.3: “To the extent Provider processes personal data subject to the GDPR or UK GDPR on Customer’s behalf, the Data Processing Addendum attached as Exhibit C applies and is incorporated into this Agreement. Provider shall not process personal data subject to the GDPR or UK GDPR unless and until Exhibit C has been executed by both parties.” Replace Exhibit C’s “[To be attached.]” with the executed DPA, which must contain the required content listed above (documented instructions; confidentiality; security measures; sub-processor conditions; assistance; deletion/return; audits and information), setting out the confirmed data types and categories of data subjects, and identifying each Customer party (Holdings, the Europe B.V., Brokerage LLC) as a controller for the data it submits — exact controller mapping is an open item (see QUESTIONS.md / STATUS.md).

clause: Exhibit A, Order Form No. 1 ¶4 (Pricing adjustments), with MSA §4.4 and §14.1
issue: The Order Form lets Provider raise fees once during the Initial Subscription Term on 60 days’ notice by up to “the greater of 8% or the change in the CPI-U.” Three breaks in one clause: (i) any unilateral increase during the initial term is prohibited outright under A3; (ii) the renewal cap is wrong in both formula and direction — provider gets the GREATER of 8% or CPI (a guaranteed ≥8% floor) versus A3’s LESSER of 5% or CPI (a guarantee of ≤5%); (iii) notice is 60 days versus A3’s 90 days. Arithmetic on the current fees ($18,500 × 12 = $222,000/yr): provider’s maximum initial-term jump = $222,000 × 8% = $17,760 (to $239,760/yr, invoiced on 60 days’ notice). Under A3 at CPI-U change of 3%: cap = lesser of $11,100 (5%) or $6,660 (3%) = $6,660. Against that example the provider formulation overcharges by $11,100/yr even before counting a mid-term increase. Actual CPI at any future date is unknown, so these are formulas plus one worked example, not a forecast.
why: A3 is a hard rule: no unilateral price increases during an initial term; renewal increases capped at the lower of 5% or CPI with 90 days’ notice. Playbook drafting note C1 (read the order form against the MSA; check the precedence clause) matters here: the increase power appears ONLY in the Order Form, and §14.1 gives the Order Form priority over the MSA for its subject matter (MSA §4.4 defers renewal fees to the Order Form) — so the fix must be made in the Order Form itself, not just in MSA §4.
redline: Replace Exhibit A ¶4 with: “4. Pricing adjustments. Fees shall not increase during the Initial Subscription Term. Provider may increase the fees for a renewal term only if it gives Customer written notice at least ninety (90) days before the end of the then-current Subscription Term, and any such increase shall not exceed the lesser of five percent (5%) or the change in the most recent twelve-month change in the CPI-U.”

clause: §2.2 (license scope) with Exhibit A; playbook names Cobalt Freight Europe B.V. and Cobalt Brokerage LLC
issue: §2.2 grants the license to “Customer only” and extends it to Affiliates only if named on an Order Form “at additional fees,” and Exhibit A names only Cobalt Logistics Holdings LLC. Client has now confirmed both affiliates WILL use the platform — Europe B.V. for Rotterdam/Hamburg routing, Brokerage LLC for carrier routing — and that Holdings signs. As drafted, affiliate use would breach the license (holding-group members are unlicensed users) or trigger an upsell. The delivered documents contain no signature blocks, so the client’s chosen compliance path (Holdings signing on behalf of the affiliates) is not yet on the paper and must be implemented in the execution version.
why: A5 is a hard rule: affiliates must be covered by the license at no additional fee, or the agreement must be signed by Holdings on behalf of affiliates. Client elected the signing path (“Holdings signs”). Note the chosen signature structure also satisfies the license-coverage prong as a backstop, and that three entities as Customer parties accept obligations joint and several-style — an inherent feature of the on-behalf structure, per the playbook.
redline: Implement the on-behalf signing structure and conform the definitions so affiliate use is licensed and authorized. (1) Signature page: “COBALT LOGISTICS HOLDINGS LLC, on behalf of itself and its Affiliates Cobalt Freight Europe B.V. and Cobalt Brokerage LLC” (all at no additional fee). (2) Add to §2.2: “An Affiliate that is a party to this Agreement as part of the signing party above is covered by the license at no additional fee.” (3) Amend §1.6 “Users”: “… Customer's employees and contractors, and the employees and contractors of any Affiliate that is a party to this Agreement as part of Customer …” (affiliate staff are not otherwise within “Customer’s employees and contractors”). Variant if GC prefers license-coverage instead: replace §2.2 with license “extends to Customer and its Affiliates, including Cobalt Freight Europe B.V. and Cobalt Brokerage LLC, at no additional fee;” both paths satisfy A5 — either can be dropped without affecting the other.

issue: Renewal terms are 24 months with non-renewal notice required at least 90 days out, versus A4’s limits of 12-month renewals and notice of 30 days or less. Missed-window economics: a missed 90-day window extends the deal 24 months at then-current rates — and with the (severed) ¶4 increase power that repricing could be ≥8%: $222,000 × 8% = $17,760, i.e., $239,760/yr locked for two years if untouched.
why: A4 is a hard rule: auto-renewal ≤ 12 months and non-renewal notice ≤ 30 days. A 24-month extension triggered by a 90-day (three-times-earlier) notice deadline is a classic silent commitment; operations teams reliably miss those.
redline: Replace §3.3: “Each Subscription Term shall automatically renew for successive renewal terms of twelve (12) months unless either party gives written notice of non-renewal at least thirty (30) days before the end of the then-current term.”

clause: Exhibit B (SLA) — “credits are the sole remedy”
issue: B5 accepts 99.5% with credits and accepts credits-as-sole-remedy only “if termination right exists for chronic failure (3 months in any 6).” No such termination right exists: Exhibit B makes credits the sole remedy for availability failures, and MSA §7.2’s only exit (termination after a failed 60-day correction) is framed around §7.1 non-conformity, not chronic SLA misses. Under the current text, a customer stuck with a flaky platform gets credits worth at most 25% of the monthly fee: $18,500 × 25% = $4,625/month ceiling — with no exit.
why: B5 is a preferred (negotiable) position, not a hard rule — this is the one non-hard item worth raising because chronic failure without an exit converts the whole subscription into an annuity for the vendor. Concede-able with Legal approval if the vendor resists.
redline: Add to Exhibit B: “If the availability target is missed in any three (3) calendar months within any six (6) consecutive calendar months, Customer may terminate the affected Order Form on written notice and receive a pro-rata refund of prepaid, unused fees.”
